A proportional hazards mortality model

Source: R/model.R
model.Rd

A model is the right-hand side of $$\log\mu = \log\mu^{\mathrm{ref}} + \sum_j \beta_j X^{(j)},$$ that is a reference mortality and the covariates whose coefficients fit() estimates. It carries nothing else: the experience data, the include, the weight and the tolerance all belong to the fit, because every candidate model in a selection exercise shares them.

A fitted model is itself a mortality, so it can be handed back as the ref_mortality of another model.

A model may carry a name. It is how compare_models() labels the candidate when the list of models does not, how diagnose() labels a lone fit, and it is printed with the model and with its fit. A name given in the list handed to compare_models() wins over the model's own.

Usage

model(ref_mortality, covariates, name = NULL)

is_model(x)

# S3 method for class 'model'
print(x, ...)

Arguments

ref_mortality

The reference mortality: a mortality, or a pronoun expression for \(\log\mu^{\mathrm{ref}}\). Anything held fixed goes here – a reference mortality is already an offset, so fixed effects need no feature of their own.

covariates

A covariates() object giving the \(X\) terms. The coefficients belong to the fit; nothing here names or supplies one.

name

An optional name for this model: a single string that is not blank, has no leading, trailing or consecutive spaces, and holds no control character such as a tab.

x

An object.

...

Ignored.

Value

model() returns a model.

is_model() returns a scalar logical.

Examples

age_shape <- variable(.x)
model(
  ref_mortality = gompertz_mortality(),
  covariates    = covariates(male = .i$male, female = !.i$male) * age_shape
)
#> <model: 2 terms>
#>   reference: ((-3.8 - (0.1 * (.i$birth - 1945-01-01.0))) + (0.09 * (.t - 2020-01-01.0)))
#>   [1] male
#>   [2] female
